content.title: What Percentage of Your Income Should Go Toward Your Mortgage?
content.text: Key Takeaways: Use the 28/36 rule as a starting point, but adjust based on your full financial picture and lifestyle. There’s no one-size-fits-all percentage. Choose a monthly payment that leaves room for savings, emergencies, and long-term goals. Determining what percentage of your income should go towards a mortgage is a crucial step in responsible homeownership. While there’s no one-size-fits-all answer, general rules and lender criteria can help you find the right balance between buying the home you want and staying financially stable. Whether you’re buying a house in Denver or browsing homes for sale in Austin, this guide will help you figure out how much mortgage you can afford – and avoid stretching your budget too thin. How to calculate your monthly percentage? There’s no perfect number that fits everyone, but a few common rules can help you decide what’s affordable and sustainable. These guidelines are based on your gross monthly income (what you earn before taxes). 1. 28% / 36% Rule This is one of the most widely used affordability benchmarks: Spend no more than 28% of your gross income on housing costs (including your mortgage, property taxes, and homeowners insurance). Keep total debt payments under 36%, including things like credit cards, student loans, and car payments. Example (Gross Monthly Income: $8,000): Housing: Max $2,240 (28%) Total Debt: Max $2,880 (36%) 2. 25% Rule This rule suggests capping your monthly mortgage payment—just principal and interest—at no more than 25% of your gross monthly income. Example (Gross Monthly Income: $8,000): Mortgage Payment: Max $2,000 (25%) This rule is often considered a more conservative approach, but it’s important to note that it doesn’t include property taxes, homeowners insurance, HOA fees, or maintenance costs. So while it can help keep your housing costs in check, you’ll still need to budget separately for those additional expenses. 3. 30% Rule Some people stretch the limit slightly, especially in high-cost cities. This rule allows up to 30% of your income for housing expenses, but make sure you still have room in your budget for other goals. Example (Gross Monthly Income: $8,000): Mortgage Payment: Max $2,400 (30%) How do lenders determine your home affordability? Mortgage pre-approval assesses your financial health to determine your borrowing limit, providing a clear house-hunting budget. Lenders assess your home affordability by evaluating a variety of factors to determine whether you can comfortably manage mortgage payments alongside your other financial obligations. Learning this information is key in determining, what percentage of your income should go to a mortgage. Here’s a breakdown of what lenders typically consider: Credit score Lenders prioritize your credit score, a key indicator of creditworthiness and financial responsibility. A higher score (ideally above 620) signals lower risk, increasing mortgage approval chances and potentially securing better interest rates. Debt-to-income ratio (DTI) Lenders use the debt-to-income (DTI) ratio to assess how much of your monthly income goes toward debt. Calculated by dividing total monthly debt payments by gross monthly income, a DTI below 43% is generally preferred, though some lenders may be flexible. This helps lenders evaluate your capacity for additional debt. Income and employment history Lenders require stable and sufficient income, usually two years in the same job or industry, for mortgage approval. Pay stubs and tax returns are common income verification documents. Down payment Your down payment impacts your loan amount, monthly payments, and interest rates. While conventional loans typically require 20% down, FHA or VA loans offer lower down payment options. Assets and savings Lenders assess assets, checking, savings, retirement, and investments to confirm financial stability. Adequate reserves demonstrate that you have a financial cushion for emergencies and can cover other expenses beyond the mortgage, such as closing costs and home maintenance. Loan type and terms Loan types (conventional, FHA, VA, USDA) vary in requirements and benefits, impacting interest rates and down payments. Lenders assess your financial readiness for homeownership, ensuring you can afford the mortgage and maintain financial health. How to lower your monthly mortgage payments When determining what percentage of income should go to a mortgage, these strategies can help you reduce your mortgage costs, save money, and achieve financial stability more quickly. Each option has its benefits, so consider your financial situation and long-term goals when deciding which strategies to pursue. Make a larger down payment: A larger down payment reduces your mortgage, lowering monthly payments and total interest, and can help you avoid private mortgage insurance (PMI). Consider the loan terms: Choosing a 15-year mortgage over a 30-year mortgage saves significant interest, though monthly payments are higher. Conversely, extending to a 30-year mortgage lowers monthly payments by spreading principal and interest over a longer term. Make extra payments: Paying extra on your mortgage principal, even small amounts, can significantly reduce the total interest paid. Consider rounding up payments or making occasional lump-sum payments. Refinance your mortgage: Refinancing your mortgage can lower monthly payments and interest costs by securing a lower rate. Compare offers, including fees, to see if it’s right for you. So, what percentage of your income should go to your mortgage? While rules like 28/36, 25%, and 30% offer guidance, your ideal percentage depends on your unique financial situation, including credit score, income, debt, and down payment. Regularly reviewing and adjusting your mortgage strategy (refinancing, extra payments, or term changes) ensures manageability and sustainability with your financial goals. Frequently asked questions Is the 28/36 rule a strict limit? No, it’s a guideline. While lenders use it for qualification, your personal comfort level and financial situation may be different. However, exceeding these percentages significantly can put a strain on your budget. Should I include utilities in the 28% housing costs? The 28% typically refers to PITI (Principal, Interest, Taxes, and Insurance). While utilities are a housing expense, they are generally not included in this specific calculation for lending purposes. However, you should factor them into your overall monthly budget. What if my income fluctuates? If your income is irregular, it’s wise to base your mortgage affordability on your lowest consistent income or average your income over a longer period to ensure you can comfortably meet payments during leaner months. Can I get a mortgage if my debt-to-income ratio is higher than 36%? It might be more challenging, but it’s not impossible. Lenders may consider other factors like a strong credit score, a large down payment, or significant savings. However, it’s generally advisable to lower your debt-to-income ratio before applying for a mortgage.
